column6: Massive and crystalline, with negligible primary porosity. Groundwater is confined to the weathered mantle and to fracture and joint sets; yields are modest and highly site-dependent, so the fracture target is the whole of the siting problem

column1: pCm
column5: Crystalline basement. Sampled against the 2017 map on a national grid this one USGS class resolves to at least ten formations: about two thirds Leonean granite (LG), a ninth Rokel River Group metasediments (Er), then Magbele and Tapr (Lkm, Lkt), Liberian granite (Lg), a mylonite zone and migmatitic gneiss
column6: Mostly the crystalline basement aquifer this toolkit is built for: no primary porosity, water in the weathered and fractured zone above fresh rock, yield following regolith thickness and the fracture set at the weathered-fresh contact. But this class is not one rock, and where it covers the Rokel River metasediments the aquifer is fracture flow in indurated beds with shales acting as aquicludes - a different target. Read the aquifer map beside it: the BGS layer separates the two where this one does not

column5: Dolerite, intruded as dykes and sheets cutting the basement
column6: A dyke is usually a barrier rather than an aquifer, but its margins are commonly fractured and its contact with the country rock can concentrate flow. The dyke itself is the wrong target; the contact beside it may be the right one
